Ujjwal: Pitch done. I want to disappear.
Reena: 😬 The chart?
Ujjwal: Revenue doubling every quarter for three years. Mrs Kapoor asked where the doubling comes from. I said "momentum".
Reena: And she said?
Ujjwal: How many new clinics per quarter, and how many people to close them? I had no numbers. She wasn't angry, just tired. Like she'd seen this slide too many times.
Reena: Ouch.
Ujjwal: Then she started doubting other slides too, even the cost page, and that one was solid.
Reena: Next time we build the line from real monthly sign-ups and show the range.
Ujjwal: Yes. Sorry, I made us look careless.

qa.q: How long did the chart show revenue doubling every quarter?
qa.a: The chart showed it for three years.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling after the pitch?
qa.a: Ujjwal was embarrassed and deflated, as the wish to disappear and the apology for making them look careless show.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal do differently with the next revenue chart?
qa.a: Ujjwal could build the line from real monthly sign-ups and show a range, so each assumption can be traced and defended.

qa.q: How might Mrs Kapoor have seen the chart?
qa.a: Mrs Kapoor probably saw a familiar, unsupported slide, and since one weak claim made her doubt the rest, the whole deck lost some trust. 🤔

grounding: The chat shows a founder presenting a doubling-revenue chart with no basis, which an investor quickly questions, lowering trust in the whole deck.

subtype: Approach: scenario plan if the money is late [Thinking]
passage:
Devika's office had lost power an hour ago, so she sat by a torch on the floor of the empty workshop, a notebook on her knee and the payroll date six weeks away. Her co-founder Urmila leaned on the door frame.
"Everyone tells me the round takes longer than promised," Devika said, tapping the page. "Usually about double. So I won't plan on one future. Case one: money arrives by month three. We keep the hiring plan. Case two: month six. We pause the extra hire and move to a smaller room. Case three: it never comes. Then we keep the core team and live off customers only."
"And the cuts for each?"
"Written beside each case, so nobody argues about them when the day comes."
Urmila nodded slowly.

qa.q: Where was Devika sitting while she wrote the three cases?
qa.a: Devika was sitting on the floor of the empty workshop by a torch.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling as she wrote out the three cases?
qa.a: Devika was anxious but steady, focused on preparing rather than hoping, which is why she wrote the cuts next to each case.

qa.q: What could Devika do next to check whether case three is workable?
qa.a: Devika could ask a few customers whether they would keep paying if the team shrank, and test the customer-only plan with real numbers.

qa.q: How might Urmila have felt seeing the three cases?
qa.a: Urmila was probably reassured, because even the worst case had a written plan, which her slow nod suggests.

grounding: The passage shows a founder who expects a funding round to run late and prepares three cases with matching cost cuts for each.

subtype: Approach: comparing term sheets on more than valuation [Thinking]
passage:
Advisor's note, Wednesday. Nazia writing about Amandeep's two offers.
Amandeep had spread two papers across my table. One offered the bigger number. The other offered less but asked for less in return.
"The big number is loud," Amandeep said, ticking a list. "But it wants two board seats, and if the company is sold, it takes its money back first. The smaller one leaves me in control of the product. And I phoned three founders they backed: the second investor answers calls at night, the first one goes quiet."
It was hard not to say which one I preferred. I asked only what else needed checking. Amandeep decided to have a lawyer read both, and to wait until Friday before answering.
— Nazia

qa.q: How many board seats did the bigger offer ask for?
qa.a: The bigger offer asked for two board seats.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel about the bigger offer?
qa.a: Amandeep was tempted but wary, shown by calling the big number loud and then listing what came with it.

qa.q: What could Amandeep add to the list before answering on Friday?
qa.a: Amandeep could add how each investor has behaved when a company had a bad year, by asking those founders directly.

qa.q: What is it like for Nazia to watch Amandeep decide?
qa.a: Nazia found it hard to stay quiet about a personal preference, and so asked only what else needed checking.

grounding: The note shows a founder comparing two offers by control, board seats, first-money-back terms and how the investors treat their founders, not only the headline figure.

subtype: Approach: checking legal terms with a lawyer [Action]
passage:
I'm Santosh, and looking back, the most useful money I spent that year was on a lawyer. The paper from the investor was twenty pages, and I had read it three times without really understanding a line about "drag-along".
So I booked an hour and a half with Siddharth, who works with startups. At the start Siddharth said, "I can explain how clauses like these generally work. What you agree to is your decision, and it's worth having someone qualified read your exact papers too."
We went clause by clause in ordinary language. When I got to the drag-along one, my shoulders came down. I understood what it meant for me if a buyer arrived.
I went home with a list of four questions, not a guess.

qa.q: How long did Santosh book with Siddharth?
qa.a: Santosh booked an hour and a half.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel after understanding the drag-along clause?
qa.a: Santosh felt relieved and less afraid, shown by the shoulders coming down.

qa.q: What could Santosh do next with the list of four questions?
qa.a: Santosh could take the questions back to Siddharth or to the investor and ask for the answers in writing before signing.

qa.q: How might Siddharth see the role in this meeting?
qa.a: Siddharth sees it as explaining how such clauses generally work and leaving the decision to Santosh, since that is what was said at the start.

grounding: The account shows a founder paying a startup lawyer to explain shareholder agreement clauses in ordinary language before signing.

subtype: Approach: revising the story after repeated no's [Revision]
passage:
Urmila: Fifteen replies, and the same line in every one. "Come back when there are customers."
Ritu: I know. I've read them again and again.
Urmila: So what are they telling us?
Ritu: That the deck isn't the problem. I've been fixing slides when I should have been finding customers.
Urmila: Then no more pitching until that changes.
Ritu: Agreed. I'll call the three clinics that tried the demo and ask if they'd sign a pilot.
Urmila: And if one says no?
Ritu: Then I ask what would make it a yes.
A month later, in the same room:
Ritu: Three pilots signed. Ready to send the new deck.
Urmila: Send it to the ones who wrote "customers".

qa.q: How many pilots did Ritu sign?
qa.a: Ritu signed three pilots.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling while reading the fifteen replies again?
qa.a: Ritu felt frustrated and a bit ashamed of polishing slides instead of the real gap, as the admission about fixing slides shows.

qa.q: What could Ritu ask a clinic that says no to a pilot?
qa.a: Ritu could ask what would need to change for a yes, which gives evidence about the gap.

qa.q: How might an investor who wrote "Come back when there are customers" see the new deck?
qa.a: That investor would see someone who listened and came back with evidence that answers the concern.

grounding: The dialogue shows a founder who stops pitching after repeated identical rejections, signs pilot customers to fill the gap and returns with better evidence.

subtype: Approach: exploring revenue as an alternative [Revision]
passage:
Subject: Could your clinic prepay for a year?

Dear Sachin,

Investor talks have dragged on for five months, and every meeting ends with "we'll get back to you". I realised I was waiting on other people for something my first customers might be able to help with.

Here is my idea. If ten clinics like yours paid for a year up front, at a lower rate than usual, that would cover one developer and the servers without any investor. Growth would be slower, but we would decide what to build. If we ever failed to deliver, the unused part would be refunded.

I feel a bit nervous asking, but I would rather ask than assume. Could we talk this week?

Jahnavi

qa.q: How long have the investor talks dragged on?
qa.a: They have dragged on for five months.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi feel about asking Sachin?
qa.a: Jahnavi feels nervous but hopeful, saying so directly and choosing to ask rather than assume.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi do if only a few clinics agree to prepay?
qa.a: Jahnavi could start with a smaller plan that those clinics cover, and use the results to ask more clinics later.

qa.q: What might Sachin weigh before agreeing to prepay?
qa.a: Sachin might weigh whether the tool is worth paying for a year ahead and whether the refund promise is enough if delivery slips.

grounding: The email shows a founder, with investor talks dragging, asking early customers about prepaid contracts and a slower path that keeps more control.

subtype: Approach: prioritising urgent versus important tasks [Thinking]
passage:
Career counsellor's note, Monday. Arnab writing about a session with Bhupen, a developer laid off last week.
Bhupen arrived with a page of jumbled tasks. I asked Bhupen to say aloud how to sort them. "Two things have dates on them," Bhupen said. "How my health cover continues after the last day, and what the leaving papers say I'm owed. Those go first. The portfolio and meeting old colleagues matter a lot, but they can wait a few days each, in order."
Bhupen's voice was tight at the start and eased as the list became three short columns.
I did not add tasks. By the end of the hour, Bhupen had rung the old company's HR and booked the portfolio for Thursday.
— Arnab

qa.q: What two things did Bhupen say had dates on them?
qa.a: Bhupen said the health cover after the last day and what the leaving papers say Bhupen is owed.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling at the start of the session?
qa.a: Bhupen was tense and worried, as the tight voice shows, and then calmer as the tasks became short columns.

qa.q: What could Bhupen do if the HR call raises questions that stay unclear?
qa.a: Bhupen could ask HR to send the answer in writing, and if something still worries Bhupen, check with a qualified adviser.

qa.q: How might the HR officer at the old company have seen Bhupen's call?
qa.a: The HR officer would see a person who had thought about what to ask, which makes the conversation easier to answer.

grounding: The note shows a laid-off developer sorting tasks into ones with dates and ones that can be staged, with the counsellor adding nothing.

passage:
Subject: My numbers, as promised

Dear Shreya,

You asked me to show the sums, so here they are. Each month: rent 26,000, EMI 14,000, money to my parents 10,000, food, bills and travel 12,000. That is 62,000. I have cancelled two video subscriptions and the gym, which took off another 1,500 already.

My savings are 3,00,000 and my severance is 1,50,000, so 4,50,000 in all. That is just over seven months.

So this hunt has an end date: I will look at the numbers again at month five, and if there is no offer by then, I will accept a temporary contract.

Seeing it on paper helped. It is a limit, not a fear.

Siddharth

qa.q: What is the total of the monthly costs?
qa.a: That is 62,000.

qa.q: How does Siddharth feel after writing out the numbers?
qa.a: Siddharth feels steadier, saying seeing it on paper helped and calling it a limit, not a fear.

qa.q: What could Siddharth do if a large unexpected bill appears in month three?
qa.a: Siddharth could redo the sums with the new cost and move the review date earlier, keeping the plan honest.

qa.q: How might Shreya feel reading the email?
qa.a: Shreya would probably feel reassured, because the plan has numbers, a review point and a fallback. 🙂

grounding: The email shows a person totalling rent, EMI and family costs against savings and severance, trimming subscriptions and setting a time limit for the job search.

passage:
Sunday night.
This week I sent 300 applications. Same CV, same cover note, name of company pasted in. I felt busy all week and thought that had to count for something.
The numbers: four automatic replies, two polite rejections, one phone call. In that call the recruiter asked why I wanted "this particular role", and I couldn't remember which company it was.
Zeenat rang and asked how it was going. I said "fine". Zeenat said three careful ones beat a hundred blind ones, and I snapped back that it wasn't helping.
Now I feel worse than on Monday. All that clicking, and nothing to show for it.
Don't know what to do tomorrow.
— Gurpreet

qa.q: How many replies were automatic?
qa.a: Four replies were automatic.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet feel at the end of the entry?
qa.a: Gurpreet feels worse and lost, saying so directly, and is unsure what to do next.

qa.q: What could Gurpreet try instead of sending hundreds of the same application?
qa.a: Gurpreet could pick a few roles, match the CV to each listing and mention something specific about each company.

qa.q: How might Zeenat have felt after Gurpreet snapped back?
qa.a: Zeenat was probably concerned and a little hurt, wanting to help but getting a sharp answer.

grounding: The diary shows a laid-off developer sending hundreds of identical applications in a week, getting few replies and feeling worse while mistaking clicking for progress.

subtype: Approach: targeted outreach through the network [Action]
passage:
"Twenty names," Hrithik said, sliding the phone across the canteen table. "Old colleagues. I've messaged all of them."
"Asking for jobs?" Noor asked.
"No. I ask what they see in the market, which teams are growing, and what those teams look for."
"That's a smaller thing to say yes to."
"Exactly. Nobody wants to be cornered."
Noor scrolled. "Bhaskar's group is hiring. Want me to introduce you?"
"Please. I was nervous about sending the first message."
Noor grinned. "Someone did the same for me once."
Two weeks later, on the phone:
"Four referrals," Hrithik said. "And all four turned into interviews."
"Good," said Noor. "Now pass it on."

qa.q: How many old colleagues did Hrithik message?
qa.a: Hrithik messaged twenty old colleagues.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel about sending the first message?
qa.a: Hrithik was nervous, saying so directly, but did it anyway.

qa.q: What could Hrithik do after the four interviews to keep the network working?
qa.a: Hrithik could thank each person who helped and share what was learned, and offer help back.

qa.q: Why might Noor be glad to help?
qa.a: Noor once received the same kind of help, so passing it on feels natural.

grounding: The dialogue shows a person messaging former colleagues for advice on hiring teams and getting four referrals that lead to interviews.
